title: SSE frame drop investigation — small-frame streaming repro notes
content:
Goal:
Short scratchpad for reproducing and debugging a class of flakes we've seen in staging: short SSE frames (<= 200 bytes) sometimes never make it to the client (or arrive merged), especially through our routing/proxy layer. I want a minimal, repeatable repro and a set of hypotheses/commands to triage where frames are lost or coalesced.

Observed behavior summary (staging):
- Client using fetch() reads partial events sometimes with missing data lines.
- Symptoms: 'data:' lines dropped or combined, client-side read callbacks not fired for some events.
- Higher frequency when payloads are small and interval between sends is < 100ms.
- More common when passing through edge proxy (nginx + sidecar) than when talking directly to node.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) TCP Nagle / coalescing + proxy buffering causing small writes to be merged or dropped when chunk boundaries are not flushed properly.
2) Http/1.1 chunked encoding optimization in proxy that re-chunks content and accidentally merges event boundaries when content-length unknown and flushes aren't honored.
3) Keepalive/connection reuse bug in our sidecar that drops the last partial buffer on certain backpressure patterns.
4) Client-side parsing bug in our fetch stream consumer (less likely because raw curl/HTTPie also show issues).

Minimal server repros (local):
1) Go server that flushes after each write (should be reliable):

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    http.HandleFunc("/sse", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
        w.Header().Set("Cache-Control", "no-cache")
        fl, ok := w.(http.Flusher)
        if !ok {
            http.Error(w, "streaming unsupported", http.StatusInternalServerError)
            return
        }
        for i := 0; i < 30; i++ {
            fmt.Fprintf(w, "event: tick\n")
            fmt.Fprintf(w, "data: {"i": %d}\n\n", i)
            fl.Flush() // important
            time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond)
        }
    })
    http.ListenAndServe(":8084", nil)
}

Command to exercise with curl:
- curl --no-buffer http://localhost:8084/sse   (should print every event on its own)

2) Python client (requests) to stream and show boundaries:

python3 - <<'PY'
import requests
from time import time
resp = requests.get('http://localhost:8084/sse', stream=True)
for chunk in resp.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True):
    if chunk:
        print(repr(chunk))
PY

3) Minimal non-flushing server (bad): write without flush and small writes
- this often reproduces the issue locally if proxy inserts additional buffering.

Node/Express non-flush example:
- This writes but doesn't call res.flush() (depending on Node setup), which may get coalesced by the kernel or proxy:

const express = require('express')
const app = express()
app.get('/sse-noflush', (req, res) => {
  res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/event-stream')
  res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'no-cache')
  let i = 0
  const t = setInterval(() => {
    res.write('data: ' + JSON.stringify({i}) + "\n\n")
    // no explicit flush in plain Node
    i++
    if (i > 30) { clearInterval(t); res.end(); }
  }, 30)
})
app.listen(8085)

Repro commands through our proxy stack (local mimic):
- Direct to server: curl --no-buffer http://localhost:8084/sse  # baseline
- Through local nginx: curl --no-buffer http://127.0.0.1:18084/sse  # nginx reverse proxy config to backend 8084
- Through envoy sidecar: (start envoy config that forwards to backend) and curl --no-buffer to envoy port

Important curl flags: --no-buffer (disable libcurl buffering), -N (same as --no-buffer), --raw sometimes helps.

Quick script to compare payload boundaries and timestamp them (bash + awk):

curl -s --no-buffer http://localhost:8084/sse | awk '{ if ($0 ~ /data:/) printf("%s	%s\n", strftime("%H:%M:%S"), $0); else if ($0=="") print "<empty-line>" }'

Observed local vs proxy differences (notes):
- Direct to Go server: each data: line arrives separated and immediately (good).
- Through nginx with default proxy_buffering on: events arrive in bursts (e.g., 5 events come at once) or sometimes last event is missing until connection close.
- Turning off proxy_buffering in nginx config -> proxy_buffering off; proxy_http_version 1.1; chunked_transfer_encoding on; helps a lot.
- Envoy config: http1/codec configuration and upstream/idle timeouts influence behavior. When upstream flushes frequently but envoy aggregates 1-2KB windows, small frames (< 200B) are batched.

Repro case that specifically triggers 'drop' (not just merge):
- Sequence: send events at 20ms interval with tiny payloads (~80 bytes) while client artificially slows reading (e.g., client sleeps 500ms before iter_lines).
- In this scenario we saw 1:1 mapping fails and some event numbers skipped in client logs.
- Reproduced consistently when a proxy with internal buffering sits between server and client and proxy has a limit on number of chunks it will forward before compaction.

Server-side logs to print chunk sizes and write syscall sizes (Linux):
- instrument server to log len(written) from Write calls and optionally enable strace -e write -p PID to see syscall sizes.
- If kernel coalescing merges writes into one syscall, we still get correct bytes on the wire but proxies may re-chunk.

Example: simple Go wrapper to log bytes written per fmt.Fprintf call: add a custom io.Writer that wraps http.ResponseWriter and logs sizes.

Client parsing sanity check (JS):
- Browser fetch example:
const r = await fetch('/sse')
const reader = r.body.getReader()
while (true) { const {value, done} = await reader.read(); if (done) break; console.log('chunk', new TextDecoder().decode(value)); }
- This raw reader shows raw chunk boundaries and can confirm if data is missing vs event parsing bug in our SSE util.

What I ran today (timestamped):
- 2026-02-16 09:10: direct Go server + curl --no-buffer -> clean stream
- 2026-02-16 09:25: nginx proxy (default conf) + curl -> batching seen (5 events in burst)
- 2026-02-16 09:37: nginx with proxy_buffering off -> near-direct behavior
- 2026-02-17 14:00: envoy sidecar (local dev config) -> merged small frames, occasionally a client skip when client slowed

Quick checks to run on staging where flakes happen:
- curl --no-buffer -v --raw "https://staging-edge.example.com/stream-endpoint" and capture raw bytes to file (hexdump) to inspect chunk boundaries.
- tcpdump or tshark on the host to capture packet stream (filter port). Check whether events are present on wire or dropped before hitting client.
- strace on backend process in staging for write() syscall sizes and counts.
- Enable debug logging on sidecar (envoy) to see if it reports buffer/flush events.

Notes / small examples of problematic SSE framing: (what client sees)
- Expected stream lines:
  event: tick
  data: {"i": 12}
  
  event: tick
  data: {"i": 13}
  
- Observed (when merged):
  event: tick
  data: {"i": 12}
  event: tick
  data: {"i": 13}
  
  (single arrival where parser sees two events still OK)
- Observed (drop-like):
  event: tick
  data: {"i": 12}
  
  event: tick
  
  (data line missing)

Hypothesis for 'missing data line' case: the proxy performs an internal re-chunking and when under memory reclamation or an internal bug it may drop the tail of a chunk. Alternatively our server sometimes writes the 'data:' line as a separate small write and the flush didn't happen (or write returned error swallowed). Need to verify both server write syscall success and proxy logs.

Next steps / TODOs:
- [ ] Reproduce in staging with tcpdump to confirm whether bytes hit the wire and where they stop.
- [ ] Add instrumentation to server to log write byte counts and syscall return values around each event write. Push small patch to canary.
- [ ] Run controlled envoy/no-envoy comparison on staging to measure drop/merge frequency.
- [ ] Add a stress harness that opens N clients and simulates slow readers and quick senders to maximize probability. (script in /tmp/repro-sse-harness.sh)
- [ ] If proxy confirmed: try config toggles: disable buffering, set "streaming_flush_interval" style options, ensure http1.1 chunked transfer preserved.
- [ ] If server confirmed: ensure we use a single Write per event (combine lines into one buffer) and flush immediately.

Notes-to-self: combining the header+event+data+"\n" into one Write reduces chances of coalescing problems: e.g., buf := fmt.Sprintf("event: tick\ndata: %s\n\n", payload); w.Write([]byte(buf)); fl.Flush()

Last manual experiment result: sending larger payloads (> 1KB) eliminated the issue in all proxy combos — suggests proxy aggregation window is a factor.

Misc commands saved:
- curl --no-buffer -v --raw https://staging-edge.example.com/stream-endpoint > raw.out
- hexdump -C raw.out | sed -n '1,200p'
- tshark -i lo -w sse.pcap "tcp port 8084" &
- strace -f -e write -p <pid> 2>&1 | tee writes.log

If I'm blocked: escalate to infra team with captures and a short "how to reproduce" bundle (direct url + envoy config + small script).

Random notes:
- Remember to try curl -N vs --no-buffer on Mac vs Linux; libcurl behavior differs.
- Check kernel TCP_CORK / Nagle interactions; sometimes setting TCP_NODELAY on sockets helps.

End of scratchpad.
